p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for eleven weeks, since Bea Kowal walked out in January, and the launch window opens at the end of January 2063.
He reopened AR 2207, the closed report on the departure stage's main valve, and put Hana and Wendell on the investigation.
He told the readiness board that on Ada's lower oxygen number his plan doesn't get air there in time, and the board gave the agency until May to verify its model.
On Ares Station the colony is on rations, and Ada's count is down to 911 days.

Then Ruth's second page came with a copy of the Petrel's old timeline, the ship she lost in 2035, and next to its valve test, in fresh green ink, was 7740-112, the same supplier and part number as the valve in AR 2207.
Wendell Price. Test conductor, sixty nine.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, with four kids in Aurora.
New in this chapter: Paloma Benavidez.

Monday, March 28, 2061. 5:30 AM. Daylight saving time had come two weeks ago and taken the mornings with it, so Sam drove out to the stand in the dark again, with the heater on high and the gas bill in his shirt pocket, folded around the number he'd written under minus nine on Friday night. 7740-112.
Wendell was in the blockhouse with the thermos lid on his knee. He didn't look around. Sam set the gas bill on the console between them, number side up.
Wendell looked at it for a while. Same family, he said. Older revision. Different poppet spring.

I worked a stand in 2034. So did a lot of people. He picked up the gas bill, folded it back along its crease, and handed it over. The lady who wrote that in green knows more about that number than I do. Ask her. She'll say she can't tell you. Ask her anyway. Then, before Sam could say anything else, You didn't drive out here at five for that. Quinn says you're doing estimates today.

Wendell reached under the console and came up with a shoebox. In it were pocket notebooks, the narrow kind with a spiral at the top, forty or fifty of them, held together in bunches by rubber bands that had gone soft with age. He took off one band and fanned the covers. Each had two dates written on it in black marker and a stand number.
Every test I ever ran, he said. Front of each page, what somebody told me it would take. Back of the page, what it took. He put the band back on. I want them back.

By seven the program room had become what Quinn called the big room, which meant every table pushed together and every wall papered over. On the long wall she'd taped up the work packages from February, four hundred and eighty of them, one card each. On the table she'd set out three pads of sticky notes in three colors, green, yellow, and red, and a sign in her neat capitals: THREE NUMBERS. NOBODY WRITES ONE.

The people who came weren't the leads. Sam had asked the leads to send the people who'd actually do the work, and most of the leads had, so the room was full of people who had never built this ship, because nobody had. Two stack technicians from the Breather lab, one of them twenty three, who kept checking her phone like it might excuse her. The lander integration crew in their high bay coveralls. A woman from the electrochemistry team who brought her own calculator. Rafa sent four software engineers and came himself, which nobody had expected. Hana sent her deputy and came at nine, which everybody had.
The twenty three year old raised her hand before anybody had said anything. What if I don't know how long it takes?
Then your red's big, Quinn said. That's information too.

By 8:15 the cards on the wall had started to grow colored tails. Over the doors the countdown clock said 692. Sam's phone buzzed once with a message from Garrett. On my way down. Bringing finance. Also, the agency's new AI scheduling assistant is going to run Halcyon this week. Hale's office loves it. Garrett
Sam's getting new scheduling software this week. We got some too, that summer on the Petrel. Listen for Wendell on the loop.

327 days before launch. oh seven hundred, first integrated schedule review. new scheduling software. every bar a different color. administrator says it looks like a quilt. oh eight fifteen, critical path runs through prop qual. isol VLV cycle tests, 3 campaigns, 14 weeks. oh eight thirty, program wants 4 weeks back. options: second shift on the stand, or overlap VLV campaign 3 with stage integration. oh nine oh five, chose both. oh nine ten, prop objects. Wendell on the loop: if campaign 3 finds something, it's already bolted in. oh nine twelve, overruled. noted his objection. he asked me to note it twice. noted it twice. thirteen hundred, new chart printed. 4 weeks of float on the last bar. very pretty. seventeen thirty, L minus 327. Wendell's truck still in the lot.

Monday, March 28, 8:40 AM. Garrett came in with a man from finance who carried a laptop open in both hands, like a tray. The man from finance set it on the end of the table and turned it so the room could see. It was the 2058 bid: every work package Tallgrass had priced to win the contract, with a duration beside each one in a column labeled BASIS OF ESTIMATE.
These priced the contract, Garrett said. The ARA accepted them. We don't need four hundred people guessing on sticky notes. We have numbers.

Quinn looked at the column. Then at the wall, where the stack technicians' cards had grown red tails nearly twice as long as the bid numbers. The twenty three year old was looking at her own card very hard.

Wendell's shoebox sat at Sam's elbow with the rubber bands on. Sam had read three notebooks over coffee. On the front of one page, in 2052, somebody had told Wendell a thermal vacuum test would take nine days. On the back it said twenty two.

Sam thanks the man from finance and asks him to stay, because the bid is useful as a check, and it is. Then he opens Wendell's shoebox on the table. Front of the page is the estimate. Back of the page is what happened. I want both. The owners write their three numbers. Quinn pairs each card with the nearest thing in the notebooks or the stand logs, and where the bid and the history disagree by more than half, the owner explains it out loud. The twenty three year old explains hers in a voice nobody can hear, and then again louder. Garrett leaves at eleven. At four he sends one line: Why are your numbers longer than mine? Quinn answers it with a photo of one notebook page, front and back.

The people who'll do the work estimate it, because they know it and because they'll own the number. Benchmarks and historical data are how you check their numbers. A range carries the uncertainty a single number hides.

Tuesday, March 29. The Breather's acceptance test would be run in a chamber in Albuquerque, at Rio Puerco Electrochemical, which built the stacks. The chamber could pull down to Mars surface pressure and chill to sixty below, and only one person at Rio Puerco had ever run a full stack in it. Her name was Paloma Benavidez. She came on the screen at ten from a lab with a whiteboard behind her that said DO NOT TOUCH PUMP 2 in three languages.
Garrett had stayed for this one. Ms. Benavidez, how long is the acceptance test? One number. I've got investors who can't read a range.
Four weeks, she said, too fast. Then, after a second, If the stacks behave.

Quinn asked her for three numbers. Paloma looked off screen at somebody, then back. Three weeks if everything went right. Four most likely. Eleven if a stack tripped at pressure and they had to warm the chamber, pull it, rebuild it, and pump down again. It's happened. Once. In the qualification unit.

Quinn does it on the whiteboard while Paloma watches. Three plus four times four plus eleven, divided by six: five weeks. Eleven minus three, divided by six: one and a third. So five. Most of the time, somewhere from three and two thirds up to six and a third. Garrett asks what most of the time means, and Quinn tells him two times in three, and he writes that down, which surprises everybody. Paloma says, Nobody's ever put my eleven in a schedule without yelling at me. Sam asks her what makes a stack trip. She talks for twenty minutes, and Quinn writes the risk register entry while she's still talking.

Three point estimating captures the uncertainty, and the PERT formula weights the most likely value while still counting the tail. Reporting the standard deviation tells people how sure you are. Then ask about the pessimistic number, because that's where the risk lives.

Wednesday, March 30. The ARA's scheduling assistant had been given every file Halcyon had ever sent the agency, and at 7:02 AM it sent back a schedule. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, forwarded it with a note: The Director has seen this. It's very encouraging.

It was beautiful. Twenty two thousand activities, resequenced, color coded by subsystem, with the departure burn on February 4, 2063, two weeks ahead of the plan, and three weeks of float in front of it. It had found real things, too. It ran two habitat thermal tests in parallel that nobody had thought to pair, and it saved four days of chamber time in Albuquerque by reordering the stack checkouts.
Garrett had it up on the big screen when Sam walked in. February 4. With float. The agency's own machine says it.

Quinn had found the assumptions on page 340 of the appendix. She'd printed that page and nothing else. All resources available 100 percent of scheduled time. Calendar: 7 day weeks. No facility maintenance windows provided. Test outcomes assumed nominal. Under that she'd written, in pencil, Wendell at Watkins and Albuquerque the same week in May. Stand seal change missing. Nobody gets sick.

It takes Quinn and two of the software engineers until Friday. They feed the assistant the real calendars: five day weeks, the seal change, Wendell's one body, Paloma's one body, the stack line's actual shifts, and the most likely test outcomes instead of perfect ones. The new run puts the burn on February 18, inside the window, with no float in front of it. It keeps both of the good ideas. The paired thermal tests survive. So do the four days in Albuquerque. Sam sends Hale one page with both schedules side by side, what the assistant assumed, what's true, and the two things it found that the team adopted, with credit. Gwen calls. So the machine was wrong. The machine was fast. It was right about two things nobody here saw. It didn't know anything we didn't tell it.

An AI schedule is an input like any other estimate. Collect and analyze the data behind it: pull out its assumptions, test them against resource calendars and the estimates of the people doing the work, and keep what holds up. You stay accountable for the schedule. Say where the tool helped.

Thursday, March 31. Quinn ran the forward and backward passes by hand first, on butcher paper on the big room floor, on her knees, with the new estimates. She said the software lied faster than she did, so she liked to know what the answer was before it told her.

For two years everybody at Tallgrass had known that the critical path ran through the stand. It was the thing the building said about itself. With the new numbers it didn't. It ran through a vacuum chamber in Albuquerque: stack fabrication, plant assembly, the Breather's acceptance test at Mars pressure, and lander integration, with zero float from end to end.
The stand, with Hana's AR 2207 investigation in it, had four weeks of float now. Three weeks ago it had been on the critical path. Hana asked to see the butcher paper herself.
The software release had three weeks of float. The install kit had four. Crew training, far down the paper, had six.
Sam stood over the paper for a long time. Who do we tell? Quinn said.

The butcher paper goes up on the big room wall, and a clean version goes to every lead by noon. Each owner gets one line: you're critical, or you have three weeks of float, or four, and here's who's behind you. Paloma calls from Albuquerque an hour later. We're the critical path? The whole ship? This month. She's quiet. Then I want to be on the Monday call. Every Monday. The software team, three weeks of float, stops working Saturdays, and Rafa says so out loud in the hall as if he'd been waiting years to.

The critical path is wherever the arithmetic puts it, often somewhere nobody was looking. Show it, show the near critical paths, and tell every owner their float. Critical owners hurry for the right reason. Owners with float stop panicking. Float you hide gets spent by accident.

Thursday, March 31, 6:30 PM. Quinn stayed late to put the resource calendars into the network, which nobody had ever done for Halcyon, because, she said, nobody had ever asked the network to know that people go home.

At 7:15 she found it. The week of May 16, Wendell was scheduled in two places. At Rio Puerco in Albuquerque, four hundred and fifty miles south, where Paloma wanted the most experienced test conductor in the program sitting the Breather's first pump down. And at Stand 2 in Watkins, where the second valve campaign for AR 2207 needed him at the console, because he was the only person who'd been there the day it twitched.
He's one guy, Quinn said. I checked.

The Albuquerque test was critical. The stand campaign wasn't. The baseline had laid it in at its late dates, in May, but its early start was April 18, so it had four weeks it could sit anywhere inside. Garrett's scheduling software had a button labeled LEVEL ALL, and Quinn's cursor was sitting on it.

Quinn moves the stand campaign up to its early start, the week of April 18, which is still inside its float window, and the end date stays where it was. Wendell sits the stand in April and the Albuquerque pump down in May. Quinn writes it up in two lines for the leads: what moved, why, and that nothing critical did. Hana reads it and pulls up the April weather history for Watkins, which nobody asked her to do, and frowns at it. April out there, she says, and doesn't finish the sentence. Wendell, told he's being moved, says, Nobody's ever checked I was one person.

Build the resource calendars, then smooth: move noncritical work within its float so the end date and critical path hold. Level only what smoothing can't resolve, and report what it did to the dates. Spending float is a real cost, so say so.

Friday, April 1. Sam flew to Albuquerque on the first flight, because it was the critical path, and because he wanted to see it. Rio Puerco Electrochemical was a long tan building near the river with cottonwoods behind it just starting to leaf. The chamber was a steel cylinder you could stand up in, with a round door like a bank vault's and a sign on it that said PUMP 2: ASK PALOMA.

Paloma was thirty four and talked fast. She showed him everything: the stack fixtures, the cold plates, the pump that sounded wrong and was supposed to, the one that sounded right and wasn't. She'd written most of the test procedure. She'd run the qualification unit herself. She was the only person in the company who had ever run a full stack at Mars pressure.
At lunch, at a picnic table under the cottonwoods, he asked who her backup was.

For what? she said. Then she understood. There's a technician who's watched me twice. My manager thinks the procedure covers it. She looked at the chamber building. It doesn't. I haven't taken a week off since 2059.

By Monday a Tallgrass electrochemist named Desmond Ruiz, twenty nine, has a badge at Rio Puerco and a desk next to Paloma's. Rio Puerco's technician joins them. Paloma is suspicious for a day and then, it turns out, relieved, because she's been the only person to call at three in the morning for two years. They start a binder called WHAT PUMP 2 WANTS. Sam adds the arrangement to the resource plan and the risk register, and Peg Sato in contracts writes it into the statement of work so it survives a reorganization. On the flight home Sam reads the first page of the binder. It says, in Paloma's handwriting, If it sounds fine, check it anyway.

Manage resource availability before it fails. A single point of failure is a risk to the project and a burden on the person. Pair a backup with them on real work, capture the knowledge, and put the arrangement in the resource plan and the contract so it lasts.

Saturday, April 2. Garrett called the meeting for nine on a Saturday, which was a thing he did when he wanted people to know he meant it. He had Hale on the speaker in the middle of the table. She was in her car somewhere, and every so often a turn signal ticked under her voice.
I have the partners in May, Hale said. I'd like to tell them the program found a week. One week. I'm not asking for a miracle.

Garrett had a plan ready. The AR 2207 campaign at the stand ran in sequence before stage integration: test the valve, then build the stage around it. Overlap them. Start integrating the stage while the campaign runs. We get the stage ready three weeks early. Easy week.

Wendell was at the end of the table in his jacket. He hadn't been asked to come, and he'd come. If the campaign finds something, he said, the stage is already bolted together around it. Nobody said anything. He looked at Sam. Write down that I said that.
Sam wrote it in his notebook. Wendell watched him do it. Twice. Sam wrote it again, under the first one, and Wendell nodded once and looked out the window at the wind sock.

Quinn slid the crash table across to Sam without a word. On the Breather's critical path, lander integration could lose a week for $350,000. Plant assembly could lose one for $500,000. The software release could lose one for $200,000, but it had three weeks of float.

Sam tells Hale she can have one week, and what it costs, and where it comes from: a second integration crew on the lander for two weeks in August, $350,000 out of contingency, through the change board on Monday. The valve campaign stays in sequence. Garrett argues for ten minutes that the overlap is free. Sam turns the butcher paper around so he can see that the stand isn't on the critical path. So my three weeks were worth nothing. On the end date, nothing. On the risk, a lot. Hale says, One week, honestly bought. I can say that. Wendell gets up and leaves without a word, and on his way past Sam's chair he puts a hand on the back of it for a second.

To shorten the schedule, compress the critical path, starting with the activity whose cost slope is lowest. Crashing lander integration buys a real week at a known price. Fast tracking the valve test adds rework risk, and the stand isn't critical, so it buys nothing at all.

Monday, April 4. The integration standup was fifteen minutes on a good day. This one was in its twenty fifth. The item was the valve command interface, the software that told MOIV-1 to open and close, and whether it was done.
It's done, Rafa said. It passed every case in the simulation. Four hundred cases. We're moving it to done on the board.
It's done when it's moved a real valve, Hana said. Your simulation thinks the valve closes in two hundred milliseconds every time. I have a report on my desk that says it doesn't always.
Then put your valve in my simulation.
I'd like it to stay on the stand, where it can't hurt anybody.
Everybody else at the standup was looking at the floor. It was the third Monday in a row they'd had some version of this, and the second time in a week the word done had meant two things in one room.

Sam stops the standup and keeps the two of them afterward with Quinn and a whiteboard. He asks each of them what done has to prove, and writes their answers down side by side, and they turn out not to be opposites. Rafa needs the logic tested fast and often. Hana needs proof against the real valve's behavior, including the bad cycle. What they write: an interface is done when it passes the simulation, and the simulation includes the valve's measured response from the stand, and it's run once against the stand article before it's flagged flight ready. Rafa says the stand runs will slow him down. Hana offers him a weekly slot on the stand article, Tuesdays, which nobody has ever been offered. Quinn tapes the definition to the wall over the standup board. That's a ground rule, Rafa says. That's a ground rule, Hana says, at the same time, and they both look annoyed about it.

Find the source of the conflict, look at what each side actually needs, and work the problem until both needs are met. That's collaborating, and it fits real stakes with a little time. Then write the result down as a ground rule the team keeps, so the fight doesn't come back every Monday.
Tuesday, April 5. 6:10 AM. Paloma called Sam's cell from the chamber floor. He could hear the cottonwoods outside. He could also hear, behind her, the absence of a sound.

Pump 2 seized at three this morning. Bearing. We were in a checkout pump down, no stacks in, nobody hurt. The spare is six weeks out from the manufacturer. A pause. It's in your risk register. I watched Quinn write it down last week.
It was. Line 418. Chamber roughing pump failure, probability 2, owner Rio Puerco, response: monitor.

At 6:40, in the program room, Sam put it on the wall. The acceptance test was supposed to start May 16. Six weeks for a pump put the test into late June, and every day of it came straight off the critical path.

Wendell read the line over his shoulder. What model? Sam told him. Wendell was quiet for a second. There's one of those in ground support stores. Building 4, back corner. From the habitat thermal vac in '58. Nobody's turned it on in three years.

By 7:30 Sam and Wendell are in Building 4 with a flashlight and a pallet jack. The pump is there, under a tarp, with a tag from 2058. Wendell plugs it into a test panel and listens to it for ten minutes with his eyes shut. She'll go. Paloma checks the flanges against the chamber drawings over video and says they match within a millimeter. By noon Peg has a loan agreement written and Rio Puerco's manager has signed it. The pump leaves Watkins on a flatbed at four and gets to Albuquerque at two in the morning, and Paloma is there in the dark to meet it. The issues log gets a new line with an owner and a date on it, and the risk register gets a note: issue opened, and a second spare pump added as a response. The critical path loses three days instead of six weeks.

Recognize when a risk becomes an issue, evaluate the impact of the impediment, and choose an intervention with the people who can help. Here the impact sat straight on the critical path, so it got worked within the hour. Then update the issue log and the register, and keep reassessing.
Tuesday, April 5, 3:00 PM. The program's first monthly status since the baseline was due to Hale and the board by Friday. It was also Sam's first status report on anything bigger than a building.

Quinn put the numbers on the wall in four lines. Stack fabrication was five working days late, on the critical path. The pump had cost three more. The software release was two weeks late, and it had started with three weeks of float. The stand was on its dates.

The lander week bought on Saturday was already promised to Hale for the partners, so it covered none of this. Net, the Breather's path was eight working days late against the baseline, with no float anywhere to absorb it.
The plan's threshold, written into it in February, said that any slip of five working days or more on the critical path went to the sponsor in writing.
Garrett had seen the wall on his way past. He stuck his head in. We're still inside the window, right? Then it's green.

The report is one page and a chart. Each slip, its cause, whether it's critical, what float is left behind it. The forecast for the Breather's path, and what it does to the launch odds Hale already has. The plan: the pump recovery, a second spare pump on order, the stack line's shift plan. Under the software line Quinn writes Two weeks of float spent, one left. Watch. Sam sends it a day early. Gwen replies at 9 PM. The Director says this status told her what to worry about. She says they usually don't. Garrett reads it in the morning and comes down to the program room. You put yellow on a page with my name on it. It was yellow. Garrett thinks about that for a moment and goes back upstairs.

Assess current progress, measure it against the baseline, and communicate status in a form decision makers can use: each variance, its effect on the critical path and end date, the float left, the forecast, and what you're doing about it. Spent float belongs in the report.

Wednesday, April 6. 5:40 AM. One way light time was five minutes and fifteen seconds. Tomorrow morning it would bottom out and start climbing again, and Quinn's note on the program calendar would come down.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3601. One way, 5 minutes 15 seconds. Margin, 874 days. Hi, Dad. Sorry about the hair. I've been up since 0300, so this is the hair you get. Everybody's fine. Start there. At 0300 the CO2 scrubber in Hab 2 tripped, and its backup didn't pick up, because of course it didn't. Eleven people asleep in there. The alarm went, and I was closest, so it was me and Teodor from the machine shop in our socks pulling the backup's controller board with the hab doors sealed. We got it running in nineteen minutes. That's well inside the limit. I want you to know it was well inside the limit. Nobody even had a headache. It's not an oxygen thing, so it doesn't change my number. It's just a sleep thing. (That's my hands. They're fine. They'll stop.). Your log about the valve. You said you reopened it. You didn't do the voice, and I noticed, and I'm not going to make a big thing out of it, except that I watched it three times instead of two. Okay. I need to tell you something, and you can't tell Hollis. Promise to the screen. I'll wait. Bay D. The old storage module past the greenhouse. Hollis said no to expanding into it in January because there aren't hours on the roster for it. So I've been doing it on my own hours. Teodor helps some nights, and a botanist named Pilar who doesn't sleep anyway. We've got racks in. We've got lights in. We've got the first trays of lettuce under them, and lettuce makes oxygen, Dad, not a lot, but it makes it. It's the only thing on this station that makes more air than it did last month. It isn't in my number. It won't be until it's finished, and I won't guess at it before then. I know what you're going to say about the hours. You'd say it to anybody else. Don't say it to me. You did nineteen years of nights in a building that wasn't even on fire. 874. Same minus nine as last time, I'm guessing. Love you. Go to work. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he paused it on her hands, the way he had in January, and looked at them for a long while, and then let it play.

At 6:30 he was in the high bay. The stack line had been on two shifts since the critical path went up on the wall, and nobody had asked them to; they'd seen the paper and decided. At 4:10 that morning the twenty three year old technician had cross threaded a manifold fitting on stack six, a small brass part, easily fixed, and sat in her car in the lot afterward with the engine running and wouldn't come back in. Quinn had found her there at five and was sitting in the passenger seat now. The rest of the line sat at the bench in the lab at the far end of the high bay, the one that smelled like a swimming pool. Nobody was talking. Two of them hadn't been home since Sunday.
He thought about a car in a lot in Bennett in January with the engine running, and about Ada's hands.

He pulls up a stool at the bench and asks what the last week has been like, and then he doesn't talk for a while. It comes out slowly. They read the critical path. They read the margin on the news. They decided the colony dies if they're a day late, and nobody told them otherwise. When they're done he tells them what he knows: the path has a recovery plan, the days lost to a pump are only days, and a cross threaded fitting at four in the morning is how you lose a month. They agree on a pace together. No shift over ten hours, nobody past six days, and the line lead calls a stop any time. Sam tells them he'll carry the date to Hale and Garrett himself, and does that afternoon, with the new shift plan and its cost in days. The twenty three year old comes in at nine with Quinn. Nobody says anything about the car. The lead gives her stack six back, and she fixes the fitting herself, slowly, and gets it right.

Servant leadership: find out what the team is carrying, remove what's in their way, and set expectations with them, including a pace that's safe. Then represent their voice upward and take the date pressure yourself. A frightened team makes mistakes, and on a ship mistakes have mass.

Thursday, April 7. Commander Yusra Haddad came out from the training center in Aurora with a printout of the network folded to the bottom of the page, where crew training ran on its own long path. Six weeks of float. She'd circled the number in pen.

Rafa wants my simulator, she said. Three weeks in May, for the Breather code runs. Garrett's office called yesterday to say my float's going in the investor deck as program reserve. Nobody's asked me about either one. They just told me.
Rafa was in the doorway behind her. The Breather's critical. The crew has six weeks. The sim is the only place we can run the control code against a full plant model.
And my crew has four people learning to install an oxygen plant on Mars from a manual nobody's written yet.
Quinn looked at Sam. Neither of them could remember the team ever agreeing whose float was whose, because they never had.

They write it in ten minutes on the whiteboard and Quinn types it up. Float belongs to the project. Anyone who wants to use it says so at standup, Quinn logs it, and the owners of both paths decide together, with Sam if they can't. Then Yusra and Rafa settle it, mostly without him. Rafa gets two weeks of simulator nights in May. The crew keeps the days. Yusra gets two of Rafa's engineers to help write the install procedures the crew needs. Sam calls Garrett's office himself and asks for the crew's float to come out of the investor deck. That's the first time anybody asked me about my own schedule, Yusra says on her way out. Mine too, Rafa says, and she gives him a look, and then she laughs.

Lead the team by setting expectations at the team level and empowering it: agree the ground rule, make float visible, and let the people who own the paths settle its use. Represent the team upward, including against a deck that quietly took its float.

Thursday, April 7. 8:10 PM. The envelope was in the mailbox, long and white, addressed in green ink, with a Golden postmark and no return address. Page three. Sam brought it in with the gas bill and a seed catalog and set it on the kitchen table against the fruit bowl, where it leaned and watched him make a sandwich.
He answered Ada first. He sat in his chair, not Grace's, under the bulb over the table, and pressed record. The bulb was still dying.

I promise to the screen. I won't tell Hollis. He held up his hand to the camera, and felt foolish, and kept it up. I'm also not going to say the thing about the hours. You're right. I'd say it to anybody else. He put the hand down. I'm going to ask you for three numbers instead. How long until Bay D is finished. If everything goes right, what you'd bet on, and if the bad things happen. I won't show anybody. I just want to know where my critical path is. He thought about it. It's you, by the way. It's been you the whole time. He didn't do the voice. He watched it back once, changed nothing, and sent it, and five minutes and fifteen seconds later it was on Mars, waiting for her morning.

Quinn's schedule on the big room wall said February 18, inside the window, with no float in front of it. It was the least encouraging thing Sam had ever signed, and he believed every line of it, and so, he'd noticed, did the people whose names were on the lines.
At 9:05 Quinn called. She didn't say hello. Have you seen the long range outlook?

He hadn't. She'd moved the second AR 2207 valve campaign up to its early start, the week of April 18, so that Wendell could sit Albuquerque in May. It had been the right call on paper and in the network, and it had given them their float back.

There's a storm coming off the Palmer Divide that week. Late season. They're saying it could be a big one. Wind, and a lot of snow, sideways. She was quiet. That's the only cold week the stand gets before June. Hana checked the history. It's April or nothing.
He drove out. He didn't decide to; he was on I-70 with the heater on before he'd thought about it, and the envelope was on the passenger seat, face down, because he'd picked it up with his keys.

Wendell's truck was in the lot. It was always in the lot. Inside the blockhouse the four screens showed the stage under its blankets, and the wind was doing what it did out here, leaning on the walls hard enough that the coffee in the thermos lid on Wendell's knee shivered in rings.
April, Wendell said, before Sam had his jacket off.
Quinn says it's April or nothing.
Quinn's right. She's usually right. It's a bad habit in a scheduler.
They watched the screens. After a while Sam asked him why he'd wanted it written down twice, on Saturday.

Wendell turned the thermos lid around on his knee a full turn before he answered. So there's two, he said. One gets lost. He didn't say anything else, and Sam, who had spent nine years on flight lines with men who answered exactly the question you asked them, didn't ask a second one.
In ten days he'd told the truth on a status report and bought a week honestly and found a pump under a tarp. A storm wouldn't care about any of it.

At midnight he drove home. The envelope rode on the passenger seat, face down, where the printout of AR 2207 had ridden face up in February. That morning, at 7:48, Mars had been as close as it would come before the ship left, five minutes and fifteen seconds away, and Quinn's note on the calendar had come down. He'd open page three at the kitchen table, where he opened all of them.
Not tonight. The wind came across the prairie with nothing to stop it between Watkins and Kansas, and somewhere south of the Palmer Divide, eleven days out, the weather was already deciding.
